{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-wa-s","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"699d47c13ec343b3f44b9e1cfe3f4a6cc89b9baa7eda9bdab13543040e722933","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-wa-class-std:lineage:51","source_registry_sha256":"9f6e1cb1188348b60e3a496c6f0991207e113d4c5c50fdea6643147e46e0832e","source_liveness_sha256":"13f9e69569c91234713e9bc57e8dbd507c97dcbcafbf4df2d8e9ff3a33c56e92"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Speed, space and time","heading":"C — Driving risk, hazard management, speed, space, merging and time","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Driving risk, hazard management, speed, space, merging and time

FACT_ID: sec12-F01 | anchor: A154
Managing risk means driving aware, predictable, smooth and skilled, and building safe habits on purpose until they become your normal style. [A154]
Source: [A154 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0154]

FACT_ID: sec12-F02 | anchor: A154
The common factors in fatal crashes are speed, impairment, distraction, unbelted occupants and inexperience. [A154]
Source: [A154 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0154]

FACT_ID: sec12-F03 | anchor: A154
In Washington, vehicle crashes are among the leading causes of death for people aged 16 to 25, a group more prone to fatal and serious injury crashes. [A154]
Source: [A154 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0154]

FACT_ID: sec12-F04 | anchor: A154
Risk awareness is the ability to spot present and possible hazards, including other road users, weather and distractions, so you can change what you do before a crash. [A154]
Source: [A154 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0154]

FACT_ID: sec12-F05 | anchor: A154
Keep your eyes scanning all the time, using peripheral vision and mirrors to track what is ahead, beside and behind you. [A154]
Source: [A154 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0154]

FACT_ID: sec12-F06 | anchor: A155
After you spot a hazard that needs a change, check behind you, because traffic there affects what you can safely do. [A155]
Source: [A155 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0155]

FACT_ID: sec12-F07 | anchor: A155
Risk can never be removed completely, but you can lower it by identifying hazards and adjusting how you drive. [A155]
Source: [A155 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0155]

FACT_ID: sec12-F08 | anchor: A155
Hazard perception is scanning for risks and identifying them before they become problems, and it calls for attention, quick decisions and fitting reactions. [A155]
Source: [A155 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0155]

FACT_ID: sec12-F09 | anchor: A155
A hazard is anything that makes you change speed or direction, from a child darting into the road to a trash can, a speed limit sign or your own driveway turn. [A155]
Why it matters: a hazard need not be dangerous; the test is whether it requires a change.
Source: [A155 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0155]

FACT_ID: sec12-F10 | anchor: A155
Hazards can be still or moving and can come several at once, and the driver must decide which one needs the most urgent response. [A155]
Source: [A155 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0155]

FACT_ID: sec12-F11 | anchor: A155
Slow down as you approach hazards to gain space and time for safe decisions. [A155]
Source: [A155 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0155]

FACT_ID: sec12-F12 | anchor: A156
Situational awareness is constantly watching everything around you and predicting what to prepare for, and the drivers behind you may be the ones most affected by your choices. [A156]
Source: [A156 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0156]

FACT_ID: sec12-F13 | anchor: A156
The hazard management routine has five steps in order: plan, communicate, check, execute and evaluate. [A156]
Source: [A156 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0156]

FACT_ID: sec12-F14 | anchor: A156
In the plan step you scan around you, including the rearview mirror, and decide whether the change you want is safe. [A156]
Source: [A156 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0156]

FACT_ID: sec12-F15 | anchor: A156
In the check step you set your position and speed so the change needs no more than medium braking, recheck mirrors, and look over your shoulder for walkers and cyclists. [A156]
Source: [A156 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0156]

FACT_ID: sec12-F16 | anchor: A156
In the execute step you make the change smoothly without surprising anyone, and in the evaluate step you review how it went and adjust next time. [A156]
Source: [A156 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0156]

FACT_ID: sec12-F17 | anchor: A157
Higher speeds make seat belts less effective and leave less time to scan for walkers, cyclists and other vehicles. [A157]
Source: [A157 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0157]

FACT_ID: sec12-F18 | anchor: A157
Speeding cuts vehicle and traction control, especially in rain or snow, and lengthens the distance needed to stop. [A157]
Source: [A157 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0157]

FACT_ID: sec12-F19 | anchor: A158
Crash impact force rises with speed, so injuries become more severe and deaths more likely. [A158]
Source: [A158 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0158]

FACT_ID: sec12-F20 | anchor: A158
A speed limit is the highest legal speed under ideal conditions, and Washington law also requires a speed that is safe for current conditions. [A158]
Why it matters: driving at the posted limit can still be unlawful when the road is wet, icy or crowded.
Source: [A158 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0158]

FACT_ID: sec12-F21 | anchor: A158
Driving below the speed limit is allowed, but going over it is illegal. [A158]
Source: [A158 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0158]

FACT_ID: sec12-F22 | anchor: A158
Slow down for sharp curves or hills with poor visibility, slippery roads, areas with pedestrians, children, cyclists or animals, parking lots, heavy traffic, narrow bridges and tunnels, and residential streets. [A158]
Source: [A158 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0158]

FACT_ID: sec12-F23 | anchor: A159
Judging space takes practice, which is why new drivers face higher risk, and space can be judged by either distance or time. [A159]
Source: [A159 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0159]

FACT_ID: sec12-F24 | anchor: A159
Near other vehicles, keep a gap to the vehicle ahead of at least twice the length of your own vehicle. [A159]
Source: [A159 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0159]

FACT_ID: sec12-F25 | anchor: A160
Merge with enough room that nobody around you must swerve, slow or stop, because squeezing into a small gap is dangerous if the car ahead brakes. [A160]
Source: [A160 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0160]

FACT_ID: sec12-F26 | anchor: A160
Drivers already on the interstate have the right-of-way, so you adjust your speed up or down and use the whole on-ramp, your signal and mirrors to find a safe gap. [A160]
Source: [A160 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0160]

FACT_ID: sec12-F27 | anchor: A160
The guide says zipper merging improves traffic flow by 60 percent and makes merging predictable, lowering the risk of crashes from sudden lane changes. [A160]
Source: [A160 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0160]

FACT_ID: sec12-F28 | anchor: A160
In a zipper merge at a lane closure, keep using both lanes until you reach the marked merge area instead of moving over early. [A160]
Source: [A160 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0160]

FACT_ID: sec12-F29 | anchor: A161
At the merge point, take turns, let one car from the ending lane go in front of you, and keep a steady speed matching the open lane. [A161]
Source: [A161 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0161]

FACT_ID: sec12-F30 | anchor: A161
Eye-lead time is the defensive habit of scanning as far ahead and to the sides as you can, using mirrors for behind, so you see hazards early and act rather than react. [A161]
Source: [A161 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0161]

FACT_ID: sec12-F31 | anchor: A161
To practice judging time, choose a marker you think is 15 seconds ahead, then count until you reach it. [A161]
Source: [A161 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0161]

FACT_ID: sec12-F32 | anchor: A162
Having enough time lets you weigh and rank decisions in traffic, which reduces panic and impulsive moves. [A162]
Source: [A162 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0162]

FACT_ID: sec12-F33 | anchor: A162
When turning across oncoming traffic, remember that approaching traffic has the right-of-way, and allowing too much time is better than too little. [A162]
Source: [A162 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0162]

FACT_ID: sec12-F34 | anchor: A162
To judge a turn gap, count the seconds an oncoming car takes from a roadside marker to clear the road you want, then use that to estimate when the next car will arrive. [A162]
Source: [A162 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0162]

Glossary: hazard — anything that requires you to change speed or direction [A155]. Hazard perception — spotting risks before they become problems [A155]. Situational awareness — watching all around and predicting what comes next [A156]. Zipper merge — alternating from two lanes into one at the merge point [A161]. Eye-lead time — how far ahead your scanning reaches [A161].
Memory aid: the routine is Please Call Coach Every Evening, for plan, communicate, check, execute and evaluate [A156].
